Schema reused byte-for-byte from fe/compat/features.json (see fe/compat/README.md) plus one additive field, source_name: the literal name this entry's construct has in src/lisp_prelude.c or fe/fe.c, or null for an entry that does not map 1:1 to a single source symbol. utils/check_lisp_compat.py uses it to verify every fe primitive, kg native, and kg prelude definition appears in exactly one manifest.

features.rationale: kg's loader resolves against kg's own bounded load-path array and package state rather than Emacs' Lisp-visible load-path with .elc/.el/no-suffix probing, which is why the resolution half is kg-policy and lives in the load-path-search row. What IS Emacs-comparable is the value: since Phase 11 `load' answers t on success, as Emacs' does, where it answered nil before (11A Decision 5; load-returns-t pins it). There is no failure return to distinguish t from -- every way kg's load can fail raises, and since 11D Part 3 an enclosing condition-case can catch it (load-error-condition-reachability). One measured difference is recorded and NOT fixed: a missing file raises a plain `error' here where Emacs raises `file-missing', a subtype of `error' carrying the operation and the path in its data. A condition-case naming `error' catches both, so the divergence costs a program only the ability to name the narrower condition; adding it means condition subtypes with an inheritance test in fe's handler search, which Phase 11 does not fund. doc/TODO.md carries it.

Emacs' `load' answers t on success; kg answered nil until Phase 11 (11A Decision 5, one line in native_load). It is a separate row from native-load because that one is kg-policy -- kg's resolution is a bounded C-side load-path array with none of Emacs' .elc/.el/no-suffix probing, so the resolution has no oracle -- while the RETURN VALUE is straightforwardly comparable and now agrees. There is no failure return to distinguish t from: every way kg's load can fail raises, and since 11D Part 3 an enclosing condition-case can catch it (load-error-condition-reachability).

Recorded by sub-plan 10C (10A Decision 7 named it as an existing row; it was not one). Emacs' `load` searches `load-path`; kg's does not. A bare name resolves to exactly one place, <config>/kg/lisp/NAME.el, and a name containing '/' is a literal path -- `require` is the only form that searches, and it searches kg's bounded C-side load-path rather than a Lisp list. comparison is kg-policy because there is nothing to compare: the search list is a bounded array of 8 directories a package cannot push onto, and Emacs' probing order (.elc, .el, no suffix) has no kg analogue -- kg tries the one suffix, which since 10C both loaders agree on. The practical shape of the divergence: an init file that does (add-to-list 'load-path DIR) then (load "pkg") works in Emacs and fails here, while (add-to-load-path DIR) then (require 'pkg) works. Documented in README.md, doc/kg.1 and doc/lisp-api.md; the bounded array is a deliberate design (see src/lisp_require.c's header), not an unimplemented feature. Phase 11 note: the failure CONDITION for a name that resolves to nothing is a plain `error' here where Emacs raises `file-missing'. Recorded, not fixed -- see the native-load row.

Closed by Phase 11 sub-plan 11D Part 3 (11A Decision 5, Shape A); recorded by the Phase 10 acceptance review before that. Emacs evaluates a loaded source file inside the dynamic extent of the calling `load', so an enclosing `condition-case' handles an error from that file. kg's lisp_eval_file() re-entered fe through FeEvaluateString, a nested run dressed as a top-level call: the error transferred to that nested run's host barrier -- kg's outermost error_jump -- past every handler lexically between the load and the raise. It now uses fe's FeTryEvaluateStringWithOptions (fe sub-plan 11C, FE_API_VERSION 7), which CONTAINS the completion and returns false with this frame still live; lisp_eval_file unwinds the bookkeeping it owns -- the depth counter, the load_buffers slot and the malloc'd buffer, three lines that were unreachable on the error path before -- and then FeResignal puts the completion back in flight in the enclosing run with its kind, condition object and message intact, where the condition-case finds it. The load_buffers array stays as the belt to that braces for the completions kg's frame recovery unwinds past a caller. Reader exhaustion was always catchable, being raised before the nested evaluator starts (test_exhaustion_catchability), and still is. The THROW half is not closed and is not the same problem: see the load-throw-reachability row.

Opened by Phase 11 sub-plan 11D Part 3, in the same commit that closed load-error-condition-reachability, because the two halves of the load barrier share a root cause and not a fix. A `throw' out of a loaded file to a `catch' around the (load ...) reaches that catch in Emacs and answers 99; here the containment barrier FeTryEvaluateStringWithOptions installs is a throw wall exactly as the protected call's is, so the throw finds no catch and becomes (no-catch load-tag 99) -- an ordinary error an enclosing condition-case can handle, but not the value the catch was waiting for. That containment is what makes the error half work, so this is a consequence of the fix and not an oversight. Closing it means Shape B: `load' becomes an fe primitive with a frame kind of its own, so the loaded forms are evaluated by the same run as the caller and no barrier stands between the throw and the catch. 11A Decision 5 rejects that by scope -- it is evaluator work, not loader work -- and doc/TODO.md carries the item.

kg-policy: Emacs' require searches a Lisp-visible load-path of directories with .elc/.el/no-suffix probing and an autoload cache, none of which kg has, so agreement with the oracle is undefined for the resolution itself; what is comparable -- returns FEATURE, no-op when already provided, errors when the file does not provide it -- kg matches and test_require_provide pins. Sub-plan 10C (10A Decision 7) closed the one place two kg loaders disagreed with each other rather than with Emacs: candidate_readable() appended '.el' unconditionally, so (require 'f "name.el") looked for name.el.el while (load "name.el") beside it worked. Both now ask lisp_io.c's lisp_has_el_suffix, the single copy of that question. test_require_el_suffix pins the fix and, deliberately, the three rules that did NOT move: a bare stem still gains .el, an absent file is still 'cannot find in load-path' (the file the old code would have found, doubled.el.el, is now unreachable and its marker stays unbound), and a FILENAME containing '/' is still literal -- neither suffixed nor searched. See also the load-path-search row for what require does that load does not.

Naming mismatch against Emacs, recorded directly in test_lisp.c's own comment ('not Emacs' make-marker, which starts detached ... Recorded as a naming mismatch worth revisiting'). Not fixed in this slice (scope discipline); a real fix is a Phase 8+ prelude/library wave, not language core, so no phase is named yet.
Process filter and sentinel callbacks get their own guarded frame: an error or throw in a callback is contained and reported on the status line, leaving the main editor loop intact.

Re-classified from supported by sub-plan 10C (10A Decision 3), because the old classification could never be true: `string-length` does not exist in the pinned Emacs at all -- the snapshot on file is `void-function (string-length)` -- so a `supported` `comparison: emacs` row was asserting that kg agrees with an oracle that raises. kg's own answer is 3, and it is the right answer for kg: `string-length` is a kg native that counts codepoints, and every expectation in the cited kg_test was measured against Emacs 31's `length` on the same strings (the test file's own header comment), UTF-8 counting included. What diverges is the *name*: Emacs spells this `length`, which kg also provides. The honest row is therefore a divergence in vocabulary, pinned by a case whose oracle record is the void-function it must stay.

05E's numeric cut leaves one float reason where the old entry had two: `%d` of the nonfinite float `(/ 1.0 0)` still refuses (kg has no bignum to print an infinity or NaN into), now solely because the operand is a nonfinite float -- not because kg had no int/float distinction to make in the first place. `(/ 1 0)` no longer shares this path: Phase 6 condition handling raises an arith-error condition object before format ever sees it.

Verified directly against the pinned oracle: (string-to-char "") is 0 in GNU Emacs 31.0.90, not nil. kg's non-empty-string case (e.g. (string-to-char "abc") = 97) already agrees with Emacs; only the empty-string edge case diverges. Not fixed in this slice (scope discipline).

Half of the number gap closed at 05E and half did not, so this stays divergent. `(type-of 1)` now reads fe's type_names[] entry for the new integer tag and answers `integer`, matching the pinned Emacs snapshot -- that is what the native-type-of case pins, and it carries "expect": "agree" so the runner requires the agreement rather than treating it as a stale divergence. But `(type-of 1.0)` answers `double` where Emacs answers `float`, and a float spelling is a number spelling, so calling the number gap closed was wrong: fe deliberately did not rename the type (the message ripple through fe's own errors, docs and manifest was out of scope for 05C-05E, recorded fe-side too). The rest of kg's vocabulary is likewise its own: `pair` for Emacs' `cons`, `nil` for nil's `symbol`, fe's callable kinds (`lambda`, `primitive`, `native-fn`, `macro`) for Emacs' `function`/`subr`, and a process wrapper answering the raw `fex0` tag. Sub-plan 10C added the native-type-of-float case, which is the half this entry claimed and no case evaluated: (type-of 1.0) is `float` in the pinned Emacs and `double` here. utils/check_lisp_oracle.py's XPASS rule is what found the gap -- the one case on file agreed with the oracle, so the divergence was recorded and untested.

kg's `let' macro normalises its binding list and hands it to fe's core bindings-list `let'. Until Phase 11 it expanded to an immediate lambda application instead, which is why a `let' over a `defvar'd name was lexical: a lambda parameter is a lexical environment entry unconditionally, in fe and -- measured -- in Emacs 31 too, so the special flag is consulted at fe's binding-list paths and nowhere else (11A Decisions 2-3). The five dynamic cases here are the 11A grid's `let' half: nested extents (A3a), `setq' inside a binding writing the binding and not the value it hides (A2a), a closure reading the value in force when it is CALLED (A5), and the restore running on a throw (A6a) as well as on an error (A6b). The last two cases are guards, not targets: a defun parameter named after a special stays LEXICAL (A4), and a name no `defvar' ever named stays lexical under `let' (A13). An implementation that made every `let' dynamic would pass every target case here and fail both guards. The macro was not deleted outright, which 11D Part 2 proposed, because fe's core form raises wrong-type-argument for the one-element binding (a) where Emacs -- and kg before this change -- answers nil for (let ((a)) a); normalising in the macro keeps that, and keeps (let ((a 1 2)) a) answering 1, kg's long-standing reading of a shape Emacs rejects.

`let*' expands to a chain of two-argument `internal--let' declarations, one per binding, so each initializer runs with the previous bindings already in force. Since Phase 11 that path is special-aware too: phase11-dynamic-let-star (11A grid probe A3b) shows the second initializer's function call seeing the first binding's dynamic value, which kg answered lexically before.

The capture/restore pair sub-plan 11D Part 4 replaced internal--save-excursion and internal--with-current-buffer with. Those two were natives that called the body as a thunk, which is what made a `throw' out of the body uncatchable outside the form; the two forms are now prelude macros over Lisp `unwind-protect' and only the editor state stays in C. (internal--excursion-capture SAVE-POINT) answers a right-gravity marker at point in the current buffer when SAVE-POINT is non-nil and the current buffer object when it is nil -- the two scopes save-excursion and with-current-buffer respectively preserve, which are the scopes the natives preserved before and Emacs' own. (internal--excursion-restore STATE) puts it back and releases it, tolerantly: a buffer killed underneath the form is a restore with nothing to restore to, not an error, because an unwind-protect cleanup that raises REPLACES the completion it was unwinding and would swallow the error that killed the buffer. The saved state is a GC-managed adapter object rather than a malloc'd record with an fe cleanup registration, so an unwind that never reaches the cleanup cannot leak one. kg-policy: Emacs has no such pair, and what IS Emacs-comparable is the behaviour of the two macros built on them.

The restore half of the pair the native-excursion-capture-restore row above describes; it is a separate row only because this manifest's source-coverage rule wants every kg native named by some entry's source_name, and one entry can name only one. The case, the tests and the reasoning are that row's.

A prelude macro over Lisp `unwind-protect' since sub-plan 11D Part 4, where it was a wrapper around the internal--save-excursion native before. The change of shape is what made a `throw' out of the body reach a `catch' outside the form (the catch-throw-reachability row); the state preserved is unchanged -- the current buffer and point in it, held by a right-gravity marker, so text inserted before the saved point carries it along. kg-policy because the state kg has to preserve is kg's; what is Emacs-comparable is the control flow through it, which the catch-throw-reachability and condition-case rows own.

A prelude macro over Lisp `unwind-protect' since sub-plan 11D Part 4, same change of shape as prelude-save-excursion above and for the same reason. It restores the current BUFFER and deliberately not point in it, which is Emacs' scope for the form -- it is save-current-buffer plus set-buffer -- and was the native's scope before. A buffer killed underneath the form is a restore with nothing to restore to rather than an error; see the native-excursion-capture-restore row for why a raising cleanup would be worse.

Closed by Phase 11 (11A Decisions 2-3); recorded as the manifest's sharpest divergence by sub-plan 10C before that. kg's `defvar' binds a value, leaves an already-bound name alone (first-defvar-wins, which the prelude-defvar case pins), and since Phase 11 also MARKS the symbol, which is what makes `let' over it dynamic. The two arities mark differently, and the difference is Emacs' measured one rather than a simplification: a two-argument `defvar' marks the symbol fully special (special-variable-p answers t -- phase11-dynamic-two-arg-defvar-special), while a one-argument `(defvar v)' sets the let-dynamic flag alone, so special-variable-p answers nil (phase11-dynamic-one-arg-defvar-not-special) and yet `(let ((v 5)) (f))' is 5 -- which is where the first approximation below is measured, in the separate row phase11-one-arg-defvar-file-scope. Binding is shallow: the binding swaps the global value cell and records the old contents -- or the fact that there were none, which is why phase11-dynamic-let-over-unbound-special sees boundp go nil again afterwards -- and the restore runs on every completion kind fe has. The headline the phase exists for is phase11-dynamic-temporary-setting-idiom: the ordinary Emacs temporary-setting idiom, written over three top-level forms, answered nil here and t in Emacs, silently. TWO APPROXIMATIONS ARE RECORDED RATHER THAN DEFENDED. First, kg's marking is GLOBAL where Emacs scopes a one-argument `defvar' to the file it appears in; a one-argument `defvar' in one kg file therefore makes the name let-dynamic everywhere, which is broader than Emacs and cannot make a correct program wrong without that program also relying on the narrower scope. That is no longer prose: phase11-one-arg-defvar-file-scope is a `divergent' row whose case pins both answers. Second, the 53 generically-named `internal--let' temporaries in lisp/prelude.el (result, res, doc, name, ...) become dynamically capturable the moment a user `defvar's such a name -- which is exactly Emacs' own exposure for lexical-binding libraries, so it is recorded, not defended (11A Decision 3). What did NOT change is as much of the design as what did: closure and defun PARAMETERS bind lexically unconditionally even when named after a special, which is Emacs 31's measured answer under lexical-binding: t and is guarded by phase11-dynamic-parameter-stays-lexical.

The one approximation Phase 11's marking model makes, recorded as a row rather than left in prose (11A Decision 2). A one-argument `(defvar v)' sets the let-dynamic flag alone in both dialects -- special-variable-p answers nil, and `let' over the name is nevertheless dynamic -- but Emacs scopes that effect to the FILE the defvar appears in, while kg marks the symbol globally. Measured both ways. In one lexical-binding: t file, `(defvar ov)' then `(defun ovf () ov)' then `(let ((ov 5)) (ovf))' as three top-level forms answers 5 in Emacs 31.0.90 and 5 in kg: they agree. Through the oracle shim, which evaluates each setup form with its own `eval FORM t' and so puts them in different scopes, Emacs answers (void-variable ov) and kg still answers 5: the divergence, in the only shape this corpus can pin it. kg is BROADER, never narrower, so no program that is correct under Emacs' rule computes something else here unless it relies on a one-argument defvar in one file NOT reaching another. Closing it needs a notion of which file a form came from, which neither fe's evaluator nor kg's loader has; doc/TODO.md carries the item. The two-argument arity has no such gap: its mark is global in Emacs too.

The value/docstring split and first-assignment behaviour the prelude-defconst case pins, plus -- since Phase 11 -- the special marking. `defconst' marks the symbol FULLY special, exactly as a two-argument `defvar' does (phase11-dynamic-defconst-special), and, exactly as in Emacs, the constancy is a declaration and not enforcement: the name is still `let'-rebindable and the rebinding is dynamic like any other special's (phase11-dynamic-defconst-rebindable). This entry carried a null rationale until Phase 11.

fe sub-plan 11B's Emacs-named predicate, answering the *special* flag alone: t for a symbol marked by a two-argument `defvar' or a `defconst', nil for one marked let-dynamic-only by a one-argument `defvar' or never marked at all (those two answers are pinned by the prelude-defvar row's cases). The case here pins the constants: Emacs answers t for t, nil and every keyword -- they are special even though nothing can ever bind one -- and fe reproduces all three, a measured extension beyond 11A's grid that fe's own commit records. source_name is null because the primitive is fe's and fe/compat/features.json owns the source row; this entry exists because the name is reachable from kg's Lisp and its Emacs comparison is kg's to run. The companion primitive `internal--mark-special' has no row here for the opposite reason: nothing but kg's own `defvar'/`defconst' macros call it, and its Emacs comparison is undefined (Emacs has no such function), so fe's manifest carries it as kg-policy.

Emacs answers `wrong-type-argument`; kg answers a `(error "wrong-type-argument")` whose car is `error`, so the handler naming the specific symbol never matches and only a generic `(error ...)` handler catches it. kg's own editor natives still raise prose through FeHandleError: sub-plan 06A's Decision 2 scoped this phase to Fe's conditions and deferred classifying kg's ~81 natives to the follow-up that gives each one its Emacs condition symbol and data. Fe's own natives are already classified, which is why `(car 1)` does match a `wrong-type-argument` handler -- the gap is kg-side and native-by-native. The kg_test pins both halves of the true behaviour.

Closed by Phase 11 sub-plan 11D Part 4 (11A Decision 6), by exactly the fix this row's own rationale named: `save-excursion' and `with-current-buffer' are prelude macros over Lisp `unwind-protect' in lisp/prelude.el, so no native frame stands between a `throw' in the body and a `catch' outside the form. They used to be natives that called the body as a thunk, and fe walls a throw search at a native re-entry boundary by design (fe/compat/features.json's throw row calls it "a tested wall"), so the throw was converted to (no-catch tag escaped) there. 06E's protected call had already made both forms transparent to `condition-case' and to quit, and that guard is kept -- test_wrapping_native_transparency asserts it still crosses both. WHAT REMAINS A WALL is every native re-entry that is not one of these two forms: hooks, process filters and sentinels, and a nested `command-execute'. Those are callbacks kg invokes from its own C, not forms a user writes around a body, so there is no prelude expansion that removes the frame; a throw out of one still becomes no-catch. Their rows say so, and README.md and doc/kg.1 were re-worded in 11E to name the two forms that now pass and the callbacks that do not.

Recorded by sub-plan 10D Part 1, after measuring the oracle rather than reading a manual. In GNU Emacs 31.0.90 a member of after-change-functions that signals is called exactly ONCE across three insertions: the error reaches the caller, Emacs empties the hook, and the later insertions are clean. kg contains the error, reports `Hook error (HOOK): MESSAGE' in the echo area, and leaves the member armed, so the same shape runs three times and reports three times -- which on a per-keystroke hook makes the buffer unusable rather than merely noisy. comparison is kg-policy because the two containment models are not comparable form for form: Emacs' disarming is a modification-hook rule specifically, while kg's containment is the mechanism that lets a C-g or a budget completion survive a hook (sub-plan 06E's protected call), and removing an entry from inside its own run would have to answer what happens to the rest of the list. Recorded, not fixed. A *package* can take Emacs' policy for itself, and the proof that it can is lisp/auto-fill.el: its hook entry point is a condition-case that stores the condition, remove-hooks itself and messages once, and the cited PTY case asserts the package's own line reaching a real screen while `Hook error' does not -- inverting the condition-case turns that case red with exactly the opposite pair.

The 04E cutover: kg now runs on the Lisp-2 fe, so defun writes the function cell and setq the value cell, and the parent plan's own headline example '(setq f 7) then (defun f () 9)' coexists -- (list f (f)) is (7 9), matching the pinned Emacs snapshot. Pre-cut kg shared one cell per symbol (fe.c: a symbol was (name . value)) and answered ((lambda nil 9) 9), which is what Phase 4 replaced.

features.kg_test: fe/test_api.c:TestMacroExpansion (Fe-side); no kg-side test names this exact re-expansion-side-effect property today
features.rationale: kg-policy rather than an Emacs-comparable divergence: Emacs macro-expands once (or once per compilation unit under byte-compilation) and the difference is a performance/step-budget property of kg's own evaluator, not a value Emacs and kg could disagree on for a pure macro -- a macro whose expansion has side effects like this one is deliberately pathological, written to demonstrate the property, not typical kg or Emacs code. Recorded per the parent sub-plan's explicit divergences-to-record-on-day-one list ('Macros expand on every invocation, charged to the step budget').

Phase 8, 08E: prelude declaration over defvar. It distinguishes an unbound variable from a bound one, does not evaluate the standard form when bound, records the docstring, and accepts inert presentation keywords (:type, :options, :group, :tag, :link, :version, :package-version). Unknown keyword and semantic keyword forms are rejected. No Custom state, retained standard form, setopt or Customize UI is provided. The rationale used to list dynamic binding among those, and since Phase 11 that is false the other way round: the expansion's `defvar' marks the symbol special, so a `let' over a `defcustom'd name uses dynamic binding like any other special's. defcustom inherits that from `defvar' and adds nothing of its own -- see the prelude-defvar row for the marking model and its two recorded approximations.

Answers the command registry's question, which is the only one kg can answer: a built-in cmdtable row, or a defun whose body carried an (interactive ...) declaration. Emacs asks the function object whether it has an interactive form and so also says t for an anonymous lambda or a keyboard macro bound to no name; kg has no interactive-form reflection (07D defers it), and Emacs' optional FOR-CALL-INTERACTIVELY argument is not accepted. The interactive-command-predicate case carries "expect": "agree": every answer it compares does agree with the oracle, which is exactly why sub-plan 10C added commandp-anonymous-lambda -- (commandp (lambda () (interactive) 1)) is t in the pinned Emacs and nil here, so the recorded divergence is now the thing a case measures rather than a sentence in this field. utils/check_lisp_oracle.py's XPASS rule found it.
Empty prefill, exactly the accepted bytes back including the empty string, no history ring, and the clause tail verbatim as the prompt.

08B implements Table C in fe core: nil, t and every keyword symbol refuse assignment with setting-constant, keywords self-evaluate, keywordp is a primitive. kg's prelude let checks the three binding names itself. It did that because a kg let compiled into a lambda application and fe lets a lambda parameter named t shadow (which is Emacs-true for a lambda and not for a let). Phase 11 (11D Part 2) moved kg's let onto fe's core bindings-list form, which refuses all three itself, so the prelude's check is a second opinion now rather than the only one -- see lisp/prelude.el's own comment and the prelude-let row. The reason to keep it is that it is what makes the message kg's users see kg's own; the reason recorded here until this cycle -- that nothing else checks -- stopped being true at Phase 11.
08E accepts and removes a declare form only in the definition macro's optional-docstring position; unknown declaration specs are inert, matching the measured subset.
08E's measured subset applies quoted global (SYMBOL VALUE) entries and rejects extra Custom metadata.

08C implements Table R's readable half: character literals with the measured control rule, #x/#o/#b radix integers, the shared string escape table, and dotted backquote. Each row is byte-identical to the pinned oracle. The rows Emacs reads and fe deliberately does not are in phase8-reader-unsupported-syntax; the printed-symbol difference in a nested backquote is in phase8-reader-backquote-symbol-names.

Emacs reads both spellings; fe raises a named read error instead, because a vector needs an object type the core does not have and #: needs uninterned symbols. The snapshots are the measured Emacs answers these rows diverge from -- [1 2 3] and (t "sym" t sym) -- not what kg does.

fe's reader spells the two backquote reader macros `quasiquote' and `unquote' where Emacs spells them ` and , (doc/fe-upstream.md's reader-macro row). The structure and the evaluated value agree -- an unquote in cdr position is a dotted tail in both -- so only an unevaluated nested backquote prints differently, which is what this snapshot records. THE QUOTE HALF OF THIS GAP IS CLOSED: since Phase 11 the writer abbreviates (quote X) back to 'X exactly as Emacs' printer does (the writer-quote-abbreviation row). Backquote stays open because it is different in kind, not because it is more of the same work. Emacs' abbreviation is over reader-produced symbols that ARE ` and , ; kg's reader produces the ordinary symbols quasiquote, unquote and unquote-splicing, so closing this means changing what the READER expands to, which breaks any Lisp that pattern-matches on quasiquote -- and Emacs' comma abbreviation is additionally context-sensitive. 11A Decision 4 rejects it by scope; doc/TODO.md carries it.

Closed by Phase 11 (11A Decision 4, implemented in fe sub-plan 11C and inherited at 11D's pin); recorded as a divergence by 10C before that. Emacs' printer abbreviates a two-element (quote X) list back to 'X -- prin1, %S, the echo area, error renderings, all of them -- and fe's writer now does the same, recursively, so (format "%S" (list 'quote 'x)) is "'x" and (format "%S" (list 'a ''b 'c)) is "(a 'b c)" on both sides. The implementation is the symmetric copy of the (function f) -> #'f block that has been in WriteObject since Phase 4, with the same discrimination measured against the pinned Emacs: exactly one element after the head and the form proper, so (quote x y), (quote) and (quote . x) all keep printing as the pairs they are. Reading 'x produces that same two-element list on both sides, which is what made this the printer's gap and not the reader's. The sibling row phase8-reader-backquote-symbol-names records the neighbouring gap for backquote, which stays open and is different in kind: fe reads ` as `quasiquote' where Emacs reads it as a distinct symbol, so closing it means changing the reader's expansion symbols and breaking any Lisp that pattern-matches on quasiquote (11A Decision 4 rejects it by scope).

08C's reject-before-implement rule, delivered: vectors, uninterned-symbol syntax, symbol escapes and unknown string escapes are named read errors rather than silent misreadings. kg-policy because the answer is an error message, which Emacs has no comparable spelling for.

08D implements Table L in lisp/prelude.el: mapc, mapconcat with its optional separator, assq, nreverse, delq, delete, add-to-list with APPEND, identity, prog2, max/min and their error conditions, and defvar's value/docstring split. Every case here answers what the pinned oracle answers.
08E implements the Table D matrix: %c UTF-8, %x/%X/%o, and width, flag and precision handling for numeric and string conversions.

Emacs accepts the +, space and # flags and N$ field numbers; kg raises `invalid format operation` for each rather than reading them as something else. (format "%c" 0) raises where Emacs writes a NUL byte, because nothing kg stores in a string may contain one -- the same rule fe's reader applies to a string escape decoding to 0. Recorded rather than fixed: Phase 8 scoped format to the directives an init file uses.

08E: loader errors surface Fe's source label and 1-based top-level line in the init status message, for a read-time error and for one raised at run time inside a function called from a later top-level form; missing files name the resolved path, with or without an explicit .el suffix. Sub-form precision remains deferred.

Phase 9 (fe sub-plan 09B) made exhaustion of kg's fixed 1 MiB arena raise the pre-built condition (arena-exhaustion), which sits under `error` in fe's hierarchy, so `(t ...)`, `(error ...)` and the name itself all catch it; before the Phase 9 pin only `(t ...)` did, because the raise path degraded the condition object to nil. A full GC root stack is (evaluation-stack-exhaustion) on the same terms. comparison is kg-policy and no oracle snapshot exists on purpose: Emacs has no arena to exhaust, so this is kg's measured behaviour pinned against itself, per the 09 set's compatibility direction. The cited kg_test drives all three handler shapes through kg's own evaluator entry point (kg_lisp_eval_string), asserts the arena is usable again afterwards and that allocation_failures counted the failure, and pins the two things that must NOT change: a budget exhaustion is still caught by nothing, and a chain rooted in a global still pins the arena (09A Decision 3 -- recorded, not rescued). test/pty/lisp-exhaustion-caught-by-name.yaml is the same contract from inside the editor.

Always prompts and ignores any prefix; one decimal token plus trailing whitespace, classified before strtoimax/strtod, re-prompting on empty input, a non-number and junk. Integer overflow becomes a double, as in fe's reader.
A supplied prefix is returned through prefix-numeric-value without prompting; with none, exactly the n path runs. Both halves are pinned so the two cannot be reversed.
The resulting path must name an existing filesystem entry and re-prompts when it does not. Nothing is opened, created, selected, or canonicalised while constructing the argument.
The same read, permitting an absent target, and still creating nothing. realpath is deliberately not used: it cannot represent a path that does not exist.
Only an existing display name, re-prompting on a miss, with blank meaning the current buffer. The read returns a name and leaves buf_current alone; only the command body may switch.

A typed name matching nothing is accepted, blank defaults to the first other-buffer candidate, and M-RET accepts typed text literally even when a completion exists -- the path picker's explicit-literal escape. M-RET is this code's alone; C-x b ignores it.

Relative names, the completion pick-list, Tab's longest-common-prefix and M-RET's explicit-literal escape are kg's existing file-picker policy, recorded as such rather than claimed as Emacs parity. Tilde is expanded exactly once.

MINIBUF_OVERFLOW raises an ordinary error naming the code, and a truncated prefix is never delivered as if it were the answer. The refusal is a count, retired once the typed text shrinks back under the cap, on the path prompt and the buffer picker alike.

Prompts are literal in this phase: Emacs passes a prompt containing % through format with the earlier interactive arguments, and kg records that interpolation as a divergence rather than treating status text as a format string. Each clause's prompt stops at its own newline.

Prompting is allowed only while executing a command from a real key/M-x context with a live fd; init loading, eval-expression without a command fd, hooks and process callbacks fail before reading input. A nested command-execute during a command may prompt once the outer prompt has closed.

With no other buffer to offer, B's blank default is the current buffer. The ring runs from buf_current + 1 through buf_current itself, so the first candidate already is "first other, else current"; the separate fallback that claimed to handle this was unreachable and is gone.

Sub-plan 09D's arena-diagnostics command, and the second entry in this manifest that is a cmdtable row rather than a native. comparison is kg-policy because there is nothing to compare against: Emacs has no fixed arena, no slot count, and no collector of fe's shape, so agreement with the pinned oracle is undefined for every field it prints. The cited kg_test asserts the *whole* rendered echo-area line in-process against a live arena: every field, the free/peak and frames/capacity pairs included, rebuilt from FeGetArenaStats' own counters and compared exactly rather than by prefix and substring, plus the `; fails 0` that must hold for a session which has only booted. Reading the counters allocates nothing and mutates no Fe state, which is what makes an exact second read legitimate. test/pty/lisp-arena-stats-command.yaml asserts the same line reaching a real terminal, including the measured 56226 slots and 1095-frame capacity of kg's 1 MiB arena at the Phase 11 pin (56224/1096 at the Phase 10 pin; the frame record the dynamic-binding work grew costs one frame slot and returns two object slots). The command is CMD_LISP_CALLABLE and not CMD_EDITS_BUFFER: kg_lisp_arena_stats() allocates nothing and mutates no Fe state, so a handler that has just caught an arena-exhaustion may call it to see how much of the arena came back -- with the caveat that allocating nothing is also what stops it provoking the collection that returns the slots, so asked immediately after an exhaustion it reports 0 free even where the data is already unreachable, which is why the PTY case evaluates (+ 1 2) in between.
Internal docstring storage helper used by defun, defvar and defconst.
mapc answers its LIST argument, not the collected results; only a side effect distinguishes it from mapcar, which is what its case exercises.
Docstrings are stored in a bounded prelude alist rather than Fe property lists.

Re-classified from `supported` by sub-plan 10C (10A Decision 6), decided against the row's own text rather than by rule. The rationale was already truthful -- "kg has no buffer-local variable namespace; both spellings are documented aliases of setq" -- but the status word is what a gate counts and a reader skims, and `supported` beside the name `setq-default` says kg does the thing the name means. It does not: `(setq-default x 1)` writes the one global binding, so a second buffer sees the write and nothing is ever restored when a buffer is killed or switched. Emacs would answer the same two values as the cited case for entirely different reasons, which is why the row is `comparison: kg-policy` and has no snapshot. `add-hook`'s LOCAL argument is real and is a separate row; this one is the variable namespace, and Sec.14's Proof 2 bullet 'buffer-local-style configuration where supported' is satisfiable only as this recorded honesty. A real buffer-local namespace is language-runtime plus buffer-lifetime work; doc/TODO.md carries it beside `setq-local`.

The parent plan's §14 Proof 3: a small higher-order package whose pure-language portions also run unchanged under Emacs 31. lisp/pipeline.el is that pure portion -- no buffer, window, key or process -- and lisp/pipeline-text.el is the editor-facing half that (require ...)s it, which is also §14's 'multiple files' bullet. The nine cases here are the measurement, not the claim: each one's setup loads the tracked lisp/pipeline.el on BOTH sides and the snapshot is the pinned Emacs 31.0.90's own answer, so `make lisp-oracle-check' fails the moment the two stop agreeing. Between them they cover every §14 bullet: Lisp-2 cells, closures, funcall, apply, catch/throw, condition-case, one-step and fixpoint macro expansion used reflectively (10B's primitives, 10A Decision 2), macro expansion used as a predicate, and the macros evaluated normally. Two of kg's then-recorded silent divergences were deliberately NOT made load-bearing in the pure file, which is what makes the agreement a property rather than a coincidence: nothing rebinds a defvar'd variable around a call (prelude-defvar), and no returned value contains a (quote X) form (writer-quote-abbreviation). Both of those closed in Phase 11 and are `supported' now, so nothing here depends on them either way; the file is left as written because what it took to make the agreement a property is the record worth keeping. Two measured constraints shaped it: a throw could not cross a native re-entry boundary (catch-throw-reachability, also closed in Phase 11 for exactly the two forms this package avoids, though every other native re-entry is still a wall), so every catch and its throws are inside one function with no wrapping native between them; and `load' resolves a bare name only in the config directory (load-path-search), which is the one of the four that still diverges, so the two files reach each other with `require'.
